title: Optimal approximation ratio for precedence-constrained makespan
formal:
Determine the infimum approximation ratio achievable in deterministic polynomial time for nonpreemptive precedence-constrained makespan minimization on an input number of identical machines:
\[\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=\inf\mathcal R,\]
where \(\mathcal R\) consists of all real \(r\ge1\) for which there exist one uniform deterministic algorithm \(A\) and constants \(K>0\), \(d\in\mathbb N\) such that for every valid instance \(I\) of bit length \(L\), the algorithm outputs a feasible schedule \(S_A(I)\) in at most \(K(L+1)^d\) steps and
\[C_{\max}(S_A(I))\le r\,\operatorname{OPT}(I).\]
The algorithm receives the entire instance before producing its schedule. The numerical answer must determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\) to absolute error at most \(1/100\), with the proof requirement stated below. The infimum need not be attained by a single algorithm.
definitions:
Instance. There are jobs \(J=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge1\), positive integer processing times \(p_j\), a positive integer machine count \(m\), and a directed acyclic graph \(D=(J,F)\). An arc \((i,j)\in F\) requires job \(i\) to finish before job \(j\) starts. Every arc is a requirement; its transitive consequences also hold. There is no promise on the shape or depth of the directed acyclic graph, and the machine count is not fixed in advance. Every job may run on every machine, and every machine takes exactly \(p_j\) units of time to process job \(j\).

Schedule and feasibility. A schedule specifies for each job a machine \(a_j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) and a nonnegative start time \(s_j\). The job occupies precisely the half-open interval \([s_j,s_j+p_j)\) on that machine. Intervals on the same machine must be pairwise disjoint, and
\[s_j\ge s_i+p_i\quad\text{for every }(i,j)\in F.\]
Execution is continuous and uninterrupted: no job may be split, preempted or migrated. Finishing one job and starting another at the same instant is allowed. All jobs are available initially subject to their precedences. There are no release dates, deadlines, communication delays, setup times, machine eligibility restrictions or other resource constraints. The schedule uses the same number of unit-speed machines as the optimum; extra machines or speed are not allowed.

Objective. The makespan is the latest completion time,
\[C_{\max}(S)=\max_{j\in J}(s_j+p_j),\qquad
\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min_{S\text{ feasible}}C_{\max}(S).\]
This is elapsed time from zero, not the sum or average of completion times. The optimum is positive and at most \(W=\sum_j p_j\). It is unchanged if start times are restricted to nonnegative integers: for any feasible schedule, retain its machine assignments and within-machine job orders and start each job as early as those orders and the precedences allow. Positive integer durations give an acyclic augmented order and integral earliest starts without increasing the makespan. Thus an optimal integer schedule exists. Having more than \(n\) machines offers no advantage, although the full encoded value of \(m\) is counted in the input length.

Encoding. For an integer \(i\ge0\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(i+1\) and set \(U(i)=1^\ell0\operatorname{bin}(i+1)\), with exactly \(\ell\) bits in the last part. Encode an instance as \(U(n)U(m)U(p_1)\cdots U(p_n)\) followed by the \(n^2\) adjacency bits of \(D\) in row-major order. Valid inputs have the stated positivity and acyclicity properties. Encode an output schedule as the list \(U(a_1)U(s_1)\cdots U(a_n)U(s_n)\), with integer starts. These are explicit binary data, not succinct circuits or value oracles. All output bits and arithmetic costs count.

Algorithms and ratios. Computation uses a finite deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite alphabet, no advice, oracle or random bits. Polynomial time is measured in the full bit length \(L\), including all durations and the machine count, not in the numeric sum of processing times. Invalid encodings may be rejected. Each algorithm defining membership in \(\mathcal R\) must halt within its fixed polynomial bound on all valid inputs and always output a feasible schedule. Its factor \(r\) must hold simultaneously for every job count, machine count, positive duration vector and precedence graph. The program and polynomial may depend on the fixed factor \(r\), but cannot be chosen separately for each instance size. No accuracy parameter is supplied to that program in this definition.

The infimum. Graham’s polynomial-time list-scheduling guarantee implies \(2\in\mathcal R\), while feasibility forces all ratios to be at least one. Hence \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The real infimum is defined even if no algorithm attains it. In particular, proving \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le u\) may establish algorithms with ratios arbitrarily close to \(u\) from above; it need not exhibit an algorithm with ratio exactly \(u\).
answer_criterion:
Specify a real number \(a\) and give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that
\[|a-\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}|\le\frac1{100}.\]
Equivalently, supply certified bounds \(\ell\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le u\) with \(u-\ell\le1/50\), and use their midpoint. An exact value with a proof of equality also qualifies. The answer may be an unambiguous mathematical expression or a certified evaluation rule; a decimal expansion is not mandatory.

Both bound directions must concern the full stated algorithm class and every permitted instance. An upper bound at a possibly unattained infimum may be justified by polynomial-time algorithms with guarantee at most \(u+\varepsilon\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\); do not assume attainment. A lower bound must exclude every uniform deterministic polynomial-time guarantee strictly below \(\ell\), not only a specific heuristic or relaxation. Known bounds, a one-sided improvement, numerical experiments, or an unevaluated restatement of the defining optimization do not suffice unless they certify the required error.

The target is unconditional. Any complexity assumption used for a lower bound must remain explicit; a conditional interval alone does not certify this unconditional numerical answer unless the additional assumption is also proved. The tolerance is benchmark acceptance and does not by itself settle whether the exact threshold equals two.
why: Precedence constraints make scheduling depend on both how much work can run in parallel and which completions unlock later jobs. The optimal approximation ratio measures the algorithmic cost of coordinating these two effects. Pinning it down would settle a central scheduling approximation boundary whose basic factor-two guarantee dates to the 1960s.

importance.reason: A central long-standing approximation question in scheduling, connecting greedy critical-path analysis, global dependency structure and conditional hardness.

progress.text: List scheduling gives the \(2-1/m\) guarantee and therefore a universal factor-two upper bound.
Classical NP-hardness yields the barrier below \(4/3\), conditional on P being different from NP for exclusion of polynomial-time approximation.
Svensson transfers near-two hardness and proves Corollary 1 under the specifically stated stronger Unique Games variant.
Das and Wiese publish a simpler quasipolynomial scheme for unit jobs on a fixed number of machines.
The exact unit-job algorithm appears at SODA and then online in TALG.
The unique-machine preprint proves constant-factor hardness in the distinct eligibility-constrained model.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected sources give the unconditional bound \(1\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), with the classical lower bound \(4/3\) requiring P≠NP. Svensson’s factor-two hardness uses the specific Bansal–Khot variant; together with P≠NP it gives only a conditional value. No inspected result certifies the unconditional threshold to absolute 1/100. Fixed-machine quasipolynomial schemes, exact unit-job algorithms and July 2026 unique-machine hardness have different computational or input scope. The later-work search was bounded, and cited long proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: The input is an entire task graph, not a stream of arrivals. A scheduler may inspect all durations and dependencies before choosing assignments and start times. It must place every job, keep each job uninterrupted, and minimize the last completion time. Changing to an online rule, preemption, machine-dependent durations or total completion time changes the problem.

Total work \(W=\sum_j p_j\) gives the lower bound \(W/m\) on any feasible makespan. The total duration \(D\) of a longest directed path in the precedence graph gives another lower bound, since that chain runs sequentially. The difficulty is that filling machines now and finishing jobs that unlock future work can call for different priorities.

Graham’s list scheduling starts available jobs according to a priority order when machines become free. A job is available after all its predecessors finish. The established bound is \(C_{\max}\le W/m+(1-1/m)D\le(2-1/m)\operatorname{OPT}\). Although this is below two for each finite \(m\), its supremum over input machine counts is two. It therefore gives the universal bound \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\), not a fixed improvement below two.

A priority example separates a poor list from algorithmic impossibility. For \(m\ge2\), take \(m(m-1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length \(m\). Listing the long job last gives makespan \(2m-1\), whereas starting it immediately and distributing the units over the other machines gives makespan \(m\), which also equals the work lower bound. This shows tightness for that list order; it has no precedence edges and does not prove hardness for every algorithm.

Classical NP-hardness excludes every factor strictly below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\). Consequently \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) implies \(4/3\le\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}\le2\). The word “unless” is essential: NP-hardness is not an unconditional proof that a polynomial-time algorithm cannot exist.

If \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\), feasible integer schedules of polynomial bit length can be found optimally in polynomial time, so \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\). Here all optimum starts lie at most at total processing time, whose binary length is polynomial in the input length. Thus an unconditional lower bound strictly above one would in particular separate P from NP. This implication explains why the numerical target must keep its assumptions visible.

Svensson proves a transfer from the approximability of a different objective: total weighted completion time on a single machine with precedences. Hardness arbitrarily close to two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit jobs. The transferred loss tends to zero, but the two scheduling objectives and their approximation parameters are not identical.

His Corollary 1 uses the Bansal–Khot Unique Games variant in Appendix Hypothesis 1. It requires a satisfiable large bipartite portion in the completeness case and an extra expansion condition in the soundness case. The paper explicitly distinguishes it from ordinary UGC and does not establish their equivalence. Together with P different from NP, this hypothesis gives inapproximability for every fixed factor below two and hence the conditional value two.

The infimum asks which ratios can be approached by finite uniform algorithms. It need not have a minimizing algorithm: \(\rho_{\mathrm{prec}}=1\), for example, would not by its definition alone assert an exact polynomial-time optimizer. Similarly, an upper bound on the infimum can be witnessed by algorithms approaching that bound. The prescribed \(1/100\) accuracy concerns the real threshold, not the approximation error of one submitted scheduling algorithm.

For unit jobs on a fixed number of machines, approximation schemes with quasipolynomial running time represent substantial progress. Das and Wiese give a simpler such scheme at ESA 2022, following earlier results. Its runtime is still not polynomial in the sense required here, and the fixed-machine, unit-duration promises do not cover all inputs in this card.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki give an exact unit-job algorithm running in \((1+n/m)^{O(\sqrt{nm})}\) time; this is subexponential when \(m=o(n)\). They also improve the exponential base in the regime \(m=\Theta(n)\). The work appeared at SODA 2025 and online in TALG in January 2026. Faster exact exponential-time algorithms do not supply a polynomial-time universal approximation ratio.

The July 2026 unique-machine preprint proves NP-hardness of every constant approximation factor for unit jobs when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. This removes assignment flexibility and is an additional input restriction on allowable schedules, absent from the present model. Its stronger hardness therefore does not contradict the factor-two algorithm for freely assignable identical machines.

The checked evidence does not locate the unconditional threshold within an interval of width \(1/50\). The known factor-two upper bound, the classical conditional lower bound and the stronger hypothesis-based value address different logical conclusions. A small improvement below two could be a major advance while still leaving the numerical acceptance target unresolved.

sentences: The problem schedules an input number of positive-duration jobs on an input number of identical machines while respecting every precedence and minimizing the last completion time.
Its target is the infimum universal approximation factor of uniform deterministic algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length.
The accepted answer must certify that real threshold within absolute error 1/100 in Lean, allowing that the infimum is not attained.
Graham’s factor-two bound survives for all inputs, while existing lower bounds keep their explicit complexity assumptions.
Fixed-machine schemes, faster exact unit-job algorithms and hardness with predetermined machine assignments do not determine the stated unconditional threshold.
